answer.abstain_reason: None of the supplied admissible-tier (T1-T4) pages carries a Nigeria-specific value for agriculture value added per worker. The World Bank DataBank table retrieved (Source 5) contains only regional/income aggregates (e.g. Africa Western and Central, Sub-Saharan Africa) and no country rows; the other World Bank and FAO pages are landing pages or metadata glossaries with definitions only. The one page carrying an actual Nigeria series (indexmundi.com) is a T5 aggregator, which under the tier rules may be used for existence facts only and never for a statistic; it also reports an obsolete vintage (constant 2010 US$, last updated 2019) rather than the current constant 2015 US$ series.
answer.construct_note: Two construct issues, neither resolvable from the supplied pages. (1) Country scope: the only Nigeria-specific figures in the retrieved material are on a T5 aggregator, which states a 2019 value of 5,591 in constant 2010 US$ for NV.AGR.EMPL.KD; the only T1 numbers available here are aggregates, e.g. Africa Western and Central at 2,438.6 and Sub-Saharan Africa at 1,495.7 for 2025 — regional aggregates are not a Nigeria figure and must not be substituted for one. (2) Definition question flagged in the census: the indicator name says 'Agriculture ... (USD)', whereas the series both countries record, NV.AGR.EMPL.KD, is defined in the T1 metadata as 'Agriculture, forestry, and fishing, value added per worker (constant 2015 US$)' — i.e. broader sector scope (ISIC Rev.4 divisions 01-03, including forestry and fishing) and a constant-2015 price basis, neither of which is stated in the indicator name or in the bare-USD cut points. Any figure eventually ratified will therefore sit on the wrong side of the naming question unless the definition is amended, and the choice of price basis materially moves the value relative to the 2500/5000 cut points (the same series in constant 2010 US$ reads ~5,591 while the constant 2015 US$ vintage is a different number that is not in these pages).
answer.quality_evidence: T1 metadata for NV.AGR.EMPL.KD (databank.worldbank.org) fully documents the definition, base period 2015, weighted-average aggregation and the reliance on ILO modelled employment estimates, and explicitly warns of 'significant limitations on the availability of reliable data' in low- and middle-income countries. That establishes the series' provenance but supplies no Nigeria observation.
answer.scale_evidence: No Nigeria-level observation available in the supplied pages. Contextual T1 aggregates for the region containing Nigeria (Africa Western and Central, 2,122.9 in 2016 rising to 2,438.6 in 2025) are heavily weighted by Nigeria but are not a Nigeria measurement and cannot be used to place the country against the cut points.
answer.rung_argument: Level withheld. A threshold indicator can only be scored from a country-specific published value for the named construct. The evidence here fails at the first rung: no admissible-tier page in this retrieval reports agriculture value added per worker for Nigeria in any year. Placing the row at, say, level 3 on the strength of the T5 aggregator's 5,591 (constant 2010 US$) would combine an inadmissible publisher, an obsolete price basis and a sector scope wider than the indicator name — three separate defects each sufficient to void the cell.

The companion metadata glossary page (Source 2) confirms the indicator code AG.YLD.CREL.KG, unit 'kg per hectare', annual periodicity and reference period 1961-2024, so the 2024 Nigeria entry is within the published series and definitionally matched.
answer.scale_evidence: National figure covering all cereal area harvested in Nigeria; WDI aggregation method is a weighted average across cereal crops.
answer.rung_argument: The value route applies: a single published figure exists for the named construct. Construct check — the quoted row is from the WDI table for indicator AG.YLD.CREL.KG, 'Cereal yield (kg per hectare)', and the row read is Nigeria (not a regional aggregate, not a neighbouring country, not a single-crop yield such as the USDA wheat MT/HA figures in Sources 5 and 6). Year check — the table column is 'Most Recent Year' and reads 2024 for Nigeria, consistent with the metadata reference period 1961-2024. Unit check — kg per hectare as published, no conversion applied. Applying the cut points: 1,558 kg/ha is above the first cut of 1500, so level 1 is passed; it is below the second cut of 3000, so the score stops at level 2.
answer.negative_finding: Level 3 would require a published Nigerian cereal yield at or above 3,000 kg/ha. Nothing in the retrieved evidence approaches that: the WDI most-recent value is 1,558 kg/ha, and the longest series available here (IndexMundi's reproduction of the same World Bank/FAO series, Source 7) shows Nigeria never exceeding 1,655.50 kg/ha in 57 years, with 1,509.00 in 2018. Nigeria therefore sits roughly 40 percent of the world 2024 value of 3,955 shown in the same table.

answer.source_title: World Bank, World Development Indicators — Employment in agriculture (% of total employment) (modeled ILO estimate), Nigeria (SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS)
answer.quote: Nigeria	2025	34
answer.data_quality_flag: ILO modelled estimate / nowcast for 2025, not a nationally reported observation; WDI metadata warns that imputed observations 'are subject to high uncertainty, and should not be used for country comparisons or rankings'. Value displayed rounded to whole percent on the country page (T5 Trading Economics renders the 2023 WDI figure as 34.31%).
answer.construct_note: The indicator name 'Employment in agriculture (%)' omits its denominator; the quoted series is explicitly '% of total employment', which is the conventional reading of the name and the series the assessment register already carries. Two scope caveats sit on the wrong side of the unratified definition: (a) the WDI/ILO 'agriculture sector consists of activities in agriculture, hunting, forestry and fishing... category A (ISIC 4)', i.e. ISIC-A rather than crop-and-livestock agriculture alone, so the figure is an upper bound on agriculture narrowly defined; (b) the 2025 value is an ILO model nowcast, not a survey measurement, even though the register classes it 'Measured'. Nigeria's own NBS Labour Force Survey (Annual Report 2023) does publish 'Branch of Economic Activity at Main Job' / 'Economic sector of main job', which would be the survey-based national alternative, but no agriculture share figure appears in the retrieved text of that PDF.
answer.quality_evidence: Publisher is the World Bank WDI, sourcing the ILO Modelled Estimates database (ILOEST) accessed January 17, 2026 — a T1 international database. Metadata glossary page (databank.worldbank.org, SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS) confirms unit of measure '% of total employment', reference period 1991-2025, and the ISIC definition of the agriculture sector. Weakness: the Nigeria 2025 point is model-imputed/projected rather than a fresh national labour force survey observation, and WDI itself cautions against country ranking on imputed points.
answer.scale_evidence: National coverage, all employed persons of working age; denominator is total employment in Nigeria. The comparable series shows Nigeria at 34% against a world figure of 26% and Sub-Saharan neighbours ranging from 30% (Senegal) to 73% (Niger), placing Nigeria in the lower half of West African agricultural employment shares.
answer.rung_argument: Level 1 requires only that a published figure for the construct exists and sits above the 45% cut; Nigeria's published figure is 34%, so the first cut (45) is passed and the row rises to level 2. The value is quoted verbatim from a T1 publisher (World Bank WDI/ILOEST) for the correct country and the correct denominator (% of total employment), so the value and its construct match are sound: 34% of Nigerian total employment is in ISIC-A. No further cut is cleared, so the assessment stops at level 2.
answer.negative_finding: Level 3 would require the agricultural employment share to fall below the 30% cut. The published 2025 figure is 34, four points above that cut, and the series trend on the same page runs from roughly the high-30s down to 34 over 2012-2025 without crossing 30. No source in the retrieved pages publishes a Nigerian figure below 30% for employment in agriculture as a share of total employment.
answer.search_trail: Started with the World Bank WDI country page for SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS filtered to Nigeria (Source 1), which carries the headline 'Nigeria 2025 34' in both the 'Selected Countries and Economies' and 'All Countries and Economies' tables. Read the DataBank Metadata Glossary entry for SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS (Source 5) to pin the denominator ('% of total employment'), the ISIC-A scope, and the modelled/imputed caveat, which is the substance of the unratified-definition question. Attempted the ILOSTAT country profile for Nigeria and the ILOSTAT data and employment topic pages (Sources 3, 6, 7) to obtain the primary ILOEST figure — all three returned Cloudflare bot-verification interstitials with no data, a dead end. Opened the NBS Nigeria Labour Force Survey Annual Report 2023 and the NLFS Q2 2024 report (Sources 4, 8) hoping for a survey-based national agriculture share; the retrieved text covers only front matter, tables of contents and introduction (Section 3.5 'Branch of Economic Activity at Main Job' and Figure 9 'Employment by economic sector of main job (%)' are listed but their values are not in the retrieved text), so no NBS figure could be quoted. answer.abstain_reason: None of the supplied pages publishes a figure for smallholder access to formal markets in Nigeria. The World Bank/NBS GHS-Panel pages (Sources 1-6) are microdata catalogue and questionnaire documentation: they show that a channel-of-sale variable exists (s11hq4 'WHO/WHAT WAS THE LARGEST BUYER/OUTLET', sa3q10 'TO WHOM DID YOU MAINLY SELL THE HARVEST OF CROP?') but publish no tabulated percentage. The only quantified statements available concern commercial orientation / share of harvest sold, not access to FORMAL market channels, and they appear only on an IDEAS/RePEc abstract page (Source 10), which the domain tiering classifies as T5 — a tier from which statistics may not be recorded. The T2 IFPRI working paper PDF (Source 7) was retrieved only as front matter and contents; no numeric result is present in the supplied text to quote.
answer.construct_note: Closest available evidence, recorded as context only and not as the cell value: the IFPRI NSSP working paper 'The relative commercial orientation of smallholder farmers in Nigeria' (Benson, Amare & Ogunniyi 2020), using nationally representative GHS-Panel 2015/16 data, reports on its RePEc/IDEAS abstract page (T5 domain) that about one-third of smallholder farming households made no crop sales at all and another third sold less than one-third of harvested crops by value. That is a COMMERCIALISATION / share-of-output-sold measure, not ACCESS TO FORMAL MARKETS: it does not distinguish formal channels (contract buyers, processors, aggregators, cooperatives, organised/regulated markets) from sales to informal itinerant traders or neighbours, which is precisely what the indicator name asserts. Likewise the GHS-Panel 2012/13 instrument records the largest buyer/outlet by network code, which would yield a channel-of-sale SHARE if tabulated — again participation in a channel, not access. The indicator census question flagged for this row is therefore live here: the only Nigerian evidence in these pages sits on the 'channel of sale / participation' side, not the 'access' side, and no published national percentage of smallholders with access to formal markets was found.

answer.value: Nigeria has no single published national all-crop post-harvest loss rate; a Nigerian government council paper reports that 30-50% of produce is lost annually (30-50% for total agricultural produce and for perishables, up to 50% for fruits/vegetables/tubers, 5-20% for grains, 13% average for cassava, 20% for fish and livestock products).

answer.construct_note: The indicator names an all-crop national post-harvest loss rate. The quoted headline sentence refers specifically to perishable produce; the same document's Table 1 applies the same 30-50% band to row 1, 'Total Agricultural Produce', i.e. an all-crop national loss estimate, and disaggregates grains at 5-20%, fish/livestock at 20% and cassava at 13%. So the source does sit on the all-crop side of the census question, but only as a broad range, not a measured rate. The narrower, better-documented alternatives sit on the wrong side of that question: APHLIS publishes cereals-only estimates for Nigeria (2021: 17.5% maize, 9.8% millet), and FAO's SDG 12.3.1a portal publishes only a sub-Saharan Africa regional food loss figure of 23.0 percent (2023), not a Nigeria value. Neither a cereals-only figure nor a regional figure is an all-crop Nigerian rate.

answer.rung_argument: Scoring is a threshold on the published loss rate with cuts at 30, 20, 12, 5 and lower being better. Level 1 requires only that a national loss figure exist and sit at or above the worst cut: the only all-crop national estimate found for Nigeria is 30-50%, whose entire range lies at or above 30, so the 30 cut is not passed and the row rests at level 1. Level 2 would require the published all-crop national rate to fall below 30%; no retrieved source places Nigeria's all-crop rate below 30%. The value is recorded as a statement rather than a number because the source publishes a band (30-50%) plus commodity-specific figures, and selecting a midpoint would give the row a precision its source does not have.

1.5.perplexity_lead:
There is **no single, published “all‑crop national post‑harvest loss rate (%)” for Nigeria** that matches the indicator name as written. Available figures are **crop‑specific** (mainly **cereals**) or **grouped by commodity class**, and often cover different scopes (e.g. grains only, or multiple crop groups), not a unified all‑crop national percentage.

Below are the closest published constructs, and how they match or diverge from the indicator’s intended “all‑crop national post‑harvest loss rate”.

---

### 1. APHLIS: National post‑harvest loss rates for **cereals only**

The African Postharvest Losses Information System (APHLIS) provides **national post‑harvest loss percentages by cereal crop**, not a single all‑crop figure.

- For Nigeria, APHLIS reports estimated **postharvest loss percentages** for **maize, rice, sorghum and millet** (dry‑weight basis). For 2021/2022, these are around:
  - **Maize:** ~17–18% loss  
  - **Rice:** ~11–12% loss  
  - **Sorghum:** ~12% loss  
  - **Millet:** ~9–10% loss[1][3][10].
- APHLIS also decomposes these losses by **value‑chain step** (harvesting, drying, threshing/shelling, transport, storage) but still **per cereal**, not across all crops

answer.abstain_reason: None of the retrieved pages publishes a figure for the share of FARMERS with access to agricultural CREDIT in Nigeria. The two closest published figures measure adjacent but different constructs: (a) IFPRI NSSP Brief 25 reports 18 percent of farm households with access to FINANCIAL SERVICES (all services, not credit), citing 2006 CWIQ data; (b) World Bank 'Rural Finance in Nigeria' reports fewer than 2 percent of RURAL HOUSEHOLDS (a population wider than farmers) with access to any institutional finance. The CGAP/World Bank smallholder survey pages supplied report financial inclusion (account ownership) among smallholders ('Only a quarter of smallholders are financially included'), not credit access. Because the two nearest proxies straddle the 10 percent cut point (2 percent vs 18 percent) and neither measures credit access by farmers, a level cannot be set without inventing a construct match the sources do not support.
answer.construct_note: Indicator name asserts share of FARMERS with agricultural CREDIT ACCESS. Nearest available evidence in the supplied pages: IFPRI (CGSpace, T2, 2010) states 'only 18 percent of farm households (mainly smallscale farmers) have access to financial services (Akramov 2009)' — right population (farm households) but wrong service scope (all financial services, not agricultural credit), and the reference year is 2006. World Bank 'Rural Finance in Nigeria' (openknowledge, T2, 2008) states 'fewer than 2 percent of rural households have access to any sort of institutional finance' — wrong population (all rural households, including non-farmers) and wrong service scope (any institutional finance). CGAP's national smallholder survey (T4 on cgap.org, T1 mirror on documents1.worldbank.org) reports that 'Only a quarter of smallholders are financially included, meaning they hold an account registered in their own name at a full-service financial institution' — this is account ownership, not credit, and is a smallholder-household unit rather than a farmer unit. All three are 'access/inclusion' or 'use' measures of finance broadly; none is a credit-access rate for farmers.

1.7.perplexity_lead:
Nigeria does **not** have a published, nationally representative indicator that directly matches the row name “Agricultural credit access (% farmers)” as defined (share of *farmers* with *access* to credit). Existing published measures for Nigeria typically refer to **smallholder households** or **rural smallholder farmers**, and often track **use/borrowing or financial inclusion**, not pure *access*. Based on available evidence, the construct match is **imperfect** and sits on the “wrong side” of the name’s access/borrow and farmer/household distinctions.

Below are the most relevant published sources, what they measure, and how they differ from the row’s name.

---

## 1. CGAP / World Bank – Smallholder Household Survey, Nigeria

answer.abstain_reason: None of the retrieved pages carries a Nigeria-specific prevalence of undernourishment (PoU) figure. answer.abstain_reason: No source in the retrieved pages publishes a national figure for the share of Nigerian farmers using climate-smart practices. The only quantified adoption shares are sub-national and measure a narrower object: a four-state/two-zone survey reporting 87.2% of farmers having adopted at least one climate-resilient crop TRAIT (not a practice basket), and a 377-household study in parts of north-western Nigeria reporting 82% adopters. Neither is nationally representative, so recording either as 'Nigeria' would convert a data gap into a confident level-5 score.
answer.source_title: CABI Agriculture and Bioscience (Springer): State of climate smart agriculture (CSA) practices in the North Central and Northwest zones Nigeria
answer.quote: The majority (87.2%) of farmers has adopted at least one climate resilient trait in crops.
answer.data_quality_flag: sub-national purposive survey samples; not nationally representative; adoption definitions differ between studies
answer.construct_note: The indicator names the share of FARMERS (country-wide) using climate-smart PRACTICES. The best available evidence differs on two axes. (1) Object: the Springer/CABI study measures farmers who 'adopted at least one climate resilient trait in crops' — a crop-genetics trait, not a practice basket such as conservation tillage, agroforestry, residue management or water harvesting. (2) Geography: it covers smallholders in four states across the North Central and Northwest zones only, not Nigeria as a whole. The second quantified source (Agricultura Tropica et Subtropica, on a domain tiered T5 here) reports that '82 % of the respondents are adopters of the CSA practices' among 377 households in some rural areas of north-western Nigeria — closer to the named construct in object, but an even narrower, non-representative geographic base. The NBS GHS-Panel Wave 5 community questionnaire (section C6B) collects community-level responses on actions taken to reduce climate-event damage (soil conservation, rainwater harvesting, tree planting, improved/heat- and drought-tolerant seeds, irrigation), and the plot-level input module records fertiliser/organic-fertiliser use, but no published tabulation of a farmer-level climate-smart-practice adoption rate appears in the retrieved pages. NASS 2023 and the 2022 NASC list 'use of agricultural inputs and technologies' as a topic but publish no CSA adoption share in the pages supplied.
answer.quality_evidence: The strongest candidate is a peer-reviewed open-access article (T2) with a descriptive-statistics design over smallholders in four states; the second is a peer-reviewed article on a low-tier hosting domain with n=377 households and a probit/treatment-effect design. Both are credible for their own study areas but neither carries survey weights making them representative of Nigerian farmers. The only T1 instruments that could produce the named construct (NBS GHS-Panel Wave 5; NASS 2023; NASC 2022) are documented in these pages at metadata/data-dictionary level only — variable lists and topic lists, with no published adoption percentage.
answer.scale_evidence: Springer/CABI study: smallholders in four states of the North Central and Northwest zones. Nazifi et al.: 377 farming households in some rural areas of north-western Nigeria. Nigeria has 36 states plus FCT and six geopolitical zones; NASS 2023 covered 767 of 774 LGAs and 152,485 designated households, indicating the scale a national estimate would require and which the cited adoption studies do not approach.
answer.rung_argument: Level withheld. A level under this threshold rule would have to rest on a published percentage for the named construct — farmers in Nigeria using climate-smart practices. The two available percentages (87.2% and 82%) would each place the cell above the 80 cut and hence at level 5, but both are sub-national convenience/purposive samples and the higher of the two measures adoption of a crop trait rather than of a practice. Scoring level 5 off either would attribute national coverage and a practice-basket meaning to evidence that has neither, which is precisely the failure mode this hold exists to prevent. Nor can a lower level be argued: nothing in the sources establishes a national rate below any cut point.
answer.negative_finding: No level, including level 1, is proposed because the pages contain no nationally scoped measurement of climate-smart practice adoption by Nigerian farmers at all — the NBS GHS-Panel and NASS pages establish that the underlying questions are asked (climate-response actions in the community module; plot input use) but publish no derived adoption share, and the two studies that do publish shares are zone- and state-limited. Level 5 specifically is not proposed because neither 87.2% nor 82% is a national estimate, and the 87.2% figure counts a climate-resilient crop trait rather than the practices the indicator names.

answer.value: FAO's RuLIS country brief for Nigeria (General Household Survey 2018-2019) finds that among owners or rights-bearers of agricultural land in Nigeria, about a third are women, with significantly more men than women holding ownership or secure rights.

answer.source_title: FAO, RuLIS country brief: Nigeria (Nigeria General Household Survey 2018-2019)
answer.quote: owners or rights-bearers of agricultural land, about a third are women.
answer.data_quality_flag: Rounded qualitative expression ("about a third") rather than a published point estimate; derived from a household survey (GHS 2018-19) and conflicts with a lower government policy claim reported in the press
answer.construct_note: The quoted FAO figure is SDG 5.a.1(b) — share of women among owners or rights-bearers of AGRICULTURAL land — i.e. it sits on the OWNERSHIP side of the unratified definition question, which matches the indicator's name ("women who own land") rather than the operator/holder alternative; the denominator is owners/rights-bearers of agricultural land, not all agricultural holders, so it is a close but not identical reading of "% holders". Two other figures in the retrieved pages do NOT measure this construct and are recorded here only as context: (a) the World Bank Gender Data Portal (DHS 2018) reports Nigeria 4.2% for "Women who own land alone (% of women age 15-49)" — a different denominator (all women of reproductive age, not landowners/holders) and restricted to sole ownership; (b) Punch (T5 news) reports the Federal Ministry of Women Affairs WEE policy stating "Only one in five landowners in Nigeria is female. This accounts for only 10 per cent of all landowners in Nigeria" — internally inconsistent, T5, and not usable for a statistic.
answer.quality_evidence: FAO RuLIS brief is an international-organisation analytical product built on the Nigeria General Household Survey 2018-2019 (a World Bank/NBS LSMS-ISA panel), computed on the SDG 5.a.1 framework; sex-disaggregated and explicitly tested for significance of male-female differences elsewhere in the brief.
answer.scale_evidence: National coverage of Nigeria (GHS-Panel 2018-19, 5 051 households, rural and urban); the brief reports the women's share among agricultural land owners/rights-bearers at national level only, with no state-level or time-series disaggregation in the retrieved text.
answer.rung_argument: Level 1 would require a value below 10 percent; the only source measuring the named construct places women's share among agricultural land owners/rights-bearers at about a third, far above 10. Level 2 would require a value between 10 and 25; again exceeded. Level 3 requires the value to exceed the 25 cut point but not the 40 cut point: "about a third" (~33) sits squarely in that band, so level 3 is the defensible rung. The value is recorded as a statement rather than a number because FAO publishes a rounded verbal share ("about a third"), not a point estimate, and converting it to 33 would give the row precision its source does not have.
answer.negative_finding: Level 4 would require published evidence that women make up more than 40 percent of agricultural land owners or rights-bearers in Nigeria. No retrieved source shows this; FAO's phrasing caps the estimate at roughly a third, and the other retrieved figures point lower still (DHS 2018: 4.2% of women aged 15-49 own land alone; Federal Ministry of Women Affairs, as reported in Punch, claims women are a small minority of landowners). No source establishes a share above 40 percent.

The best T1 evidence in the supplied pages is national: ITU's Nigeria dashboard reports population covered by at least a 3G mobile network (2022) at 87% and population covered by at least a 4G mobile network (2022) at 81%, plus mobile-cellular network coverage of 94%. These are whole-population figures with no urban/rural split, so they cannot stand in for rural coverage — in Nigeria the coverage gap is concentrated precisely in rural and remote LGAs, so a national figure will overstate the rural value by an unknown margin. The one rural-disaggregated ITU figure visible on that page is a different indicator entirely: households with Internet access at home, rural (2017) 2%. On the unratified definitional question flagged in the indicator census: this row should be judged against RURAL as named, which means the Egypt-style national at-least-3G number is not admissible here; ITU does publish 'Population covered by a mobile-cellular and a mobile-broadband network, total and by urban/rural area' as a global/regional time series (per the ITU Statistics page), but that is an aggregate release, not a Nigeria country value, and no Nigeria rural cell appears in any supplied page.

answer.value: Nigeria's federal government, through the Nigerian Consumer Credit Corporation (CREDICORP), has launched a national digital device credit programme offering smartphones, laptops and other digital devices to working Nigerians on credit, following a pilot phase.

answer.quote: The Federal Government, through the Nigerian Consumer Credit Corporation (CREDICORP), has launched a national digital device credit programme that would make smartphones, laptops, and other essential digital tools more affordable for working Nigerians.
answer.data_quality_flag: Existence fact taken from a national newspaper report of a government statement (T5); no primary CREDICORP or gazette document was among the supplied pages, and the numbers reported in the article (pilot of 'over 1,000', scaling to 'over 15,000') are not admissible as statistics at this tier
answer.construct_note: The scheme is device FINANCING (subsidised-access credit), not a price subsidy, and it is targeted at 'working Nigerians' generally rather than at farmers or rural users. This sits precisely on the census's unresolved question: the indicator name fixes neither a targeting test nor a subsidy requirement. Note it is a state-sponsored programme run by a federal corporation, not merely a commercial telco handset instalment plan, so it would qualify under either the strict (public scheme) or loose (any financing) reading. No agriculture- or rural-specific device financing scheme appears in any supplied page. Context: the Nigerian National Broadband Plan 2020-2025 (T3) lists 'Funding & Incentives' and 'Demand Drivers' pillars, but only the table of contents and glossary were retrieved, so no device-affordability provision could be quoted; GSMA (T4) handset-affordability reports name the Nigerian Communications Commission only as a consulted organisation, with no Nigerian scheme described in the retrieved text.
answer.rung_argument: Absent is ruled out: a named national device credit programme exists. Announced is exceeded: the article reports not an intention but a launch. Adopted is exceeded: an implementing structure is named (CREDICORP working through E-Finance Company with technology support from Credlock) and a pilot has already been run and closed. Operating is therefore the rung: devices have actually been placed with users under the credit plan and a scaled phase has begun. Operating = 3; quality_evidence empty and scale_evidence empty, so no increments; proposed_level = 3.
answer.negative_finding: Level 4 was not proposed because nothing in the supplied pages is an independent or official assessment of how the scheme performs — there is no evaluation, audit, repayment-performance report or service standard, only the implementer's own launch narrative relayed by a newspaper. Level 5 was not proposed because the only reach figures available ('over 1,000' in the pilot, 'over 15,000' targeted) come from a T5 news page, where statistics are inadmissible, and the 15,000 figure is in any case a target rather than realised reach; no official disbursement, beneficiary or geographic-coverage data was found.

3.3.name: National farmer registry

answer.value: Nigeria has a formally adopted but not yet operating national farmer registry: the FMAFS/NIMC NIN-enabled farmer registry and G2P card project (announced January 2025), with a National Digital Farmers Registry still in design as of the November 2025 national stakeholder workshop and its establishment financed under the World Bank AGROW project approved in March 2026.
answer.source_title: National Identity Management Commission (NIMC), Press Release: FMAFS/NIMC NIN-Enabled Farmer Registry & G2P Card Project
answer.quote: The Federal Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security (FMAFS) in collaboration with the National Identity Management Commission (NIMC), is introducing the National Identity Number (NIN) enabled farmer registry and Government-to-People (G2P) card initiative.
answer.data_quality_flag: Implementing agencies' own announcements; no independent evaluation or enrolment statistics located
answer.construct_note: The evidence describes a register of individual farmers anchored on each farmer's National Identification Number and biometrics, which matches the indicator's name (a register of farmers as individuals). Note the same ambiguity flagged in the indicator census: the Nigerian design links each farmer's NIN to their farmland and holding characteristics ('the size of the holding, type of crops or livestock') and is bundled with a G2P benefit card, so future scale figures could mix cards issued, holdings mapped and farmers enrolled. No such figures are published yet, so no unit-mixing problem arises in this record.
answer.rung_argument: Absent is ruled out: two government sources (FMAFS ministry news, NIMC press release) and a World Bank press release describe a national farmer registry initiative for Nigeria. Announced is exceeded: beyond a statement of intent, there is an inter-agency arrangement with an institutional basis — FMAFS acting 'guided by Mr President's circular on the use of National Identification Number (NIN) by all MDAs', a defined partnership in which NIMC supplies the foundational identity ecosystem and FMAFS owns the registry, a national stakeholder workshop convened under the FG–IFAD Digital Innovation Action Plan (November 2025), and approved IDA financing under the AGROW project which will 'establish a national digital farm and farmer registry'. That is Adopted: a decided, institutionally anchored and financed programme. Base level for Adopted is 3; quality_evidence and scale_evidence are both empty, so no increments apply.
answer.negative_finding: Operating was not proposed because nothing in the retrieved pages shows the registry actually enrolling or serving farmers. The November 2025 FMAFS item reports the launch of a 'National Stakeholder Workshop on Best Practices' — i.e. a design/harmonisation step, not a live register — and the workshop report's contents list is dominated by 'Strategic recommendations' and 'Key Enablers', including an MVP still to come. The World Bank's March 2026 press release uses the future tense ('will ... establish a national digital farm and farmer registry'), which indicates no operating national registry at that date. Quality_evidence was left empty because only the implementers' own descriptions of intended function (transparency, eliminating ghost beneficiaries) are available — design, not audited performance. Scale_evidence was left empty because no enrolment, card-issuance or coverage figures are published in any retrieved source; the AGROW '"up to one million smallholder farmers"' figure is a project beneficiary target, not registry reach.
answer.search_trail: Reviewed all ten supplied pages in order. Source 7 (NIMC, T3) gave the strongest formal artifact — the FMAFS/NIMC NIN-enabled farmer registry and G2P card project, January 2025 — and is the quoted source. Source 6 (FMAFS ministry site, T3) confirmed the November 2025 National Digital Farmers Registry stakeholder workshop, NIN/NIMC anchoring and geo-tagging design, but reported no enrolment figures. Source 2 (World Bank press release, T1) confirmed the registry is still to be established under AGROW, which is decisive against an Operating rung. Sources 1 and 3 (AGROW PID, T1) were truncated before any registry component text, so no registry-specific quote was available there; Source 4 is only a document landing page with no substantive text. Sources 8 and 9 (FMAFS e-Library) returned HTTP 500 errors; Source 5 (ScienceDirect) returned a captcha wall. Source 10 (ndfrplatform.ng workshop report) is T5 by domain and in any case contains no enrolment or evaluation figures, so it was not used for scale or quality. No T1–T3 page in the set carries a count of registered farmers, so scale remains unrecorded.

answer.quote: the process generated Nigeria’s first set of land accounts for
answer.data_quality_flag: Capacity-building exercise co-produced with donors; land use classification and monetary valuation explicitly deferred to future analysis
answer.construct_note: The indicator name ('Satellite/EO data integration') fixes neither the object nor the bar. The evidence recorded here sits on the INSTITUTIONAL-ARRANGEMENTS-plus-first-output side of that open question, not the 'routine national crop maps' side: it is EO/geospatial data integrated into an official statistical product (land cover accounts) by a standing multi-agency Technical Working Group under the NBS, with NASRDA and the Federal Ministry of Agriculture & Food Security as members. It is land cover accounting, not agricultural crop mapping. Agriculture-specific EO work found in these pages is at project/workshop stage: NASRDA's own page (T3, central.nasrda.gov.ng, March 2026) describes a three-day IrrEO workshop whose expected outcome is to 'establish a clear roadmap for integrating Earth observation tools into Nigeria’s agriculture and irrigation development strategies' — i.e. a roadmap, not an operating service. FAO GIEWS publishes ASIS/VHI Earth-observation indicators for Nigeria, but that is an FAO-run global product, not evidence of Nigerian national integration.
answer.rung_argument: Absent is ruled out: multiple official Nigerian bodies (NASRDA, NBS, Federal Ministry of Agriculture & Food Security) are documented as using or hosting EO/geospatial data. Announced is exceeded: beyond statements of intent, a formal multi-agency Technical Working Group led by the NBS exists and has been convened, and NASRDA is named as the national partner institution for EO agricultural mapping. Adopted is reached: the institutional arrangement is in place under the Climate Change Act (2021) mainstreaming objective and it has produced a concrete, published national output — Nigeria's first land accounts for the nation and two states — derived from satellite land-cover datasets. Level therefore 3 (Adopted), with no addition from quality or scale fields, both of which are left empty.
answer.negative_finding: Operating was not proposed: the quoted document presents a first-time, donor-supported, capacity-building production with land use classification and monetary valuation deferred, and with the sub-national work confined to two pilot states — there is no evidence in the supplied pages of a recurring, institutionalised national EO service (e.g. routine national crop-type or irrigated-cropland maps issued on a schedule). The agriculture-specific EO initiatives (IrrEO, EO for Crop Type Mapping) are at workshop and roadmap stage in 2026. quality_evidence left empty: no independent evaluation, audit, accuracy assessment or performance report on Nigeria's EO products appears in these pages — only the implementers' own descriptions. scale_evidence left empty: no published figures for users, coverage of an operating service, or beneficiaries; the GBP 3 million IrrEO grant is an input, and 'three focus countries' and '~90% rainfed cultivation' are context, not reach of a delivered EO service.
answer.search_trail: Read all ten supplied pages in tier order. (3) FAO AGRISurvey news on NASS 2023 — household/holding survey, no EO component mentioned; not the construct. (4) FAO GIEWS Earth Observation country page for Nigeria — genuine EO indicators covering Nigeria but produced and operated by FAO globally, so it evidences FAO capability, not Nigerian national integration; carried no Nigeria-specific statistic in the retrieved text. (5) FAO Egypt crop-mapping training — different country, excluded outright. (6) MDPI Sustainability EO/SDG review — global literature review, no Nigeria-specific integration figure. (7) AfricaRice CGSpace record on rice area/yield estimation in Nigeria by remote sensing — a research report landing page, titled 'Preliminary results', with no findings text in the retrieved page, so nothing quotable and evidence of research rather than institutional integration. (8) NASRDA IrrEO workshop page (T3) — agriculture-specific but roadmap/workshop stage; used as context in construct_note. (9) RMRDC/NASRDA data-integration meeting (T3) — raw materials statistics, not agriculture, and at consultation stage. (10) Space in Africa (T5) — news, usable for existence only, adds project detail but no admissible statistic. No published Nigerian figure on the reach or measured accuracy of an operating national EO agricultural service was found in the supplied pages.

gates.reason: The indicator name conjoins three qualifiers — open, machine-readable, AI-ready. The retrieved evidence supports only part of that. MACHINE-READABLE: the NBS catalogue study pages offer structured metadata in 'DDI/XML' and 'JSON' and anonymised microdata files, which is machine-readable metadata at minimum. OPEN: the catalogue header on every retrieved page reads 'NBS Website | Register | Login' and access is via a 'GET MICRODATA' request flow; the catalogue's own License search facet carries no stated licence in the retrieved text, so the datasets are registration-gated public-use files rather than openly licensed open data. AI-READY: nothing in the retrieved Nigeria pages evidences bulk/API delivery, versioned pipelines, harmonised machine-readable data dictionaries or a machine-readable licence — the only AI-readiness criteria in the sources come from a NOAA (United States) presentation, which is not evidence about Nigeria and was not applied to any Nigerian dataset. No Nigerian general open-data portal (e.g. a national data.gov catalogue) page was supplied, so the 'open portal' side of the census's open question could not be tested. The evidence therefore sits on the statistical-microdata side of the unresolved definition, not on the open/AI-ready side.

answer.construct_note: The evidence is the primary legal instrument itself (NDP Act 2023) plus the regulator's implementing directive (GAID 2025), which is exactly the named construct: a data protection/privacy law for Nigeria.
answer.rung_argument: Absent is ruled out: a general data protection instrument exists and is published by the government regulator (NDP Act 2023; earlier NDPR 2019 issued by NITDA under the NITDA Act 2007). Adopted is exceeded: an implementing regulator is standing up machinery — the NDPC issued the General Application and Implementation Directive 2025 under 'SECTIONS 1(A), 6(C), 61 & 62 OF THE NIGERIA DATA PROTECTION ACT 2023', with articles on registration of data controllers/processors of major importance, compliance audit returns filing, DPO designation, breach notification and complaints, and the NDPC website operates live services (breach reporting, controller/processor registration, DPCO licensing, audit filing). Department of Agric-Extension and Rural Development, University of Ibadan, Ibadan Correspondence contact detail: folakeadelakun@gmail.com. Abstract: Digital agriculture technologies have the potential to increase the efficiencies and productivity of farmers. However, the use of these digital technologies requires its users to have some level of digital skills – digital literacy. This study, therefore examined the level of digital literacy of crop farmers in Oyo state. A multistage sampling procedure was used in selecting 120 respondents from the study area. A structured questionnaire was used to collect primary data. Data were analysed using descriptive (frequency, percentage, and mean) and inferential statistics (Chi-square and PPMC) were used. Results reveal that majority of the respondents were male (70%), married (90.8%), had no formal education (42.5%), with a mean age of 56 years and average farming experience of 25 years. About 79.0% had between 0.5 and 8 acres of farmland, 68.3% did not practice mixed farming, 73.3%had never used social media, and 72.5% used feature phones. Furthermore, 57.5% had a favourable perception of the use of digital tools with low knowledge (55%) of basic concepts and processes of digital agriculture and platforms. The level of digital literacy (71.7%) among crop farmers in Oyo state was low. Lack of training to develop digital skills ranked the most severe constraint to digital literacy and usage among respondents. However, the perception of the use of digital tools was favourable. The digital literacy level of crop farmers was generally low. There is a need for government to establish a digital literacy initiative specifically targeted at farmers to develop and improve their digital skills through training. The NBS Labour Force Survey pages supplied contain only table-of-contents and introductory text, with no occupational breakdown of ICT-in-agriculture roles by sex, and the NAERLS/FMAFS Agricultural Performance Survey page supplied lists chapter headings only, with no sex-disaggregated extension-staff counts. Recording any of these as the named construct would convert a data gap into a scored value.
answer.construct_note: Closest available evidence sits on the wrong side of the census's open question in two ways at once. (1) Population: the CTA/Dalberg-derived figure describes women as roughly a quarter of registered USERS of digital agriculture services, i.e. farmers being served, not people EMPLOYED in digital-ag roles (extension staff, agtech-company employees, or ICT-in-agriculture occupations). (2) Geography: that figure is sub-Saharan-Africa-wide, not Nigeria-specific, and Rule 5 forbids importing a regional or other-country figure as a Nigerian one. Nigeria's national labour statistics (NBS NLFS) do disaggregate employment by sex but at aggregate/sector level, not for any digital-agriculture occupational category; the supplied NLFS pages carry no such table in any case. No admissible source in the retrieved set defines or counts a Nigerian digital-ag workforce, so the denominator the indicator presupposes does not exist in the evidence.

answer.scale_evidence: No numerator (women in digital-ag roles) and no denominator (total digital-ag workforce) is published for Nigeria in any retrieved page. answer.rung_argument: No level is proposed. 6.1.name: Global Innovation Index

answer.value: WIPO's Global Innovation Index 2025 places Nigeria 105th of 139 economies, with published GII pillar scores for Nigeria ranging from 14.85 (Human capital and research) to 31.51 (Business sophistication) and five of the seven pillars below 27.
answer.unit: GII pillar score (0-100 scale); overall composite score not published on retrieved pages
answer.source_title: WIPO, Nigeria Ranking in the Global Innovation Index 2025
answer.quote: Nigeria ranks 105th among the 139 economies featured in the GII 2025.
answer.data_quality_flag: Retrieved WIPO pages publish Nigeria's GII rank and its seven pillar scores, but not the single overall GII composite score; the only page carrying an explicit overall 'Innovation Index' figure (17.10 for 2024) is a T5 aggregator, which is inadmissible for a statistic.
answer.construct_note: The evidence is the Global Innovation Index for Nigeria, published by WIPO, the index owner. It differs from the indicator's expected form in that the admissible pages give a rank (105th of 139, GII 2025) and disaggregated pillar scores rather than the single overall GII score against which the 25/35/45/55 cut points are set. A T5 aggregator (countryeconomy.com) lists Nigeria's overall index as 17.10 for 2024 and 18.40 for 2023; that figure is recorded here only as context and is not used as the value, since T5 sources may support existence facts but never statistics.
answer.quality_evidence: WIPO is the publisher and owner of the Global Innovation Index; the economy page is the authoritative country brief. It states the 2025 rank (105th of 139), the six-year rank series (117th 2020, 118th 2021, 114th 2022, 109th 2023, 113rd 2024, 105th 2025), the input/output sub-index ranks (127th inputs, 80th outputs) and the statistical confidence interval for the rank (92 to 110). The companion benchmark page publishes Nigeria's scores in all seven GII pillars.
answer.scale_evidence: From the WIPO benchmark page for Nigeria (GII 2025): Institutions 26.66; Human capital and research 14.85; Infrastructure 25.32; Market sophistication 17.42; Business sophistication 31.51; Knowledge and technology outputs 19.77; Creative outputs 18.26. Top-10 comparator scores on the same page range from 54.93 to 78.63, showing the scale is the same 0-100 metric on which the overall GII score is expressed. Six of Nigeria's seven pillar scores fall at or below 26.66 and the mean of the seven is about 21.
answer.rung_argument: Level 1 requires the GII value to sit below the first cut point of 25. The construct is confirmed for Nigeria by the index publisher itself (WIPO), so this is not a data gap. On the value: the overall GII score is, by WIPO's own method, an average of the Innovation Input Sub-Index (mean of the first five pillars) and the Innovation Output Sub-Index (mean of the last two). Every one of Nigeria's five input pillars is at or below 31.51, with four at or below 26.66, and both output pillars are below 20; the seven published pillar scores average about 21. No arithmetic combination of these published components can reach 25. The rank corroborates this: 105th of 139 economies, 11th of 32 in Sub-Saharan Africa, in a year when the top-10 pillar averages run 55-79. The evidence therefore places Nigeria unambiguously below the first cut point, i.e. level 1. No single overall figure is quoted because none appears on the admissible pages, so a statement rather than a manufactured number is recorded.
answer.negative_finding: Level 2 would require a published GII score of 25 or above. Nothing in the admissible WIPO pages shows Nigeria at or above 25 on any aggregate measure: only one of seven pillar scores (Business sophistication, 31.51) exceeds 25, and both output pillars plus Human capital and research, Market sophistication and Infrastructure sit below it. Nigeria also falls below the Lower middle-income group average in Institutions, Human capital and research, Infrastructure and Market sophistication, so no pathway to a 25-plus composite is evidenced.
answer.search_trail: Started with the WIPO GII country brief for Nigeria (gii-ranking/en/nigeria, GII 2025) as the index owner's own page: it carries the rank (105th of 139), the 2020-2025 rank series and the tracker, but no overall composite score. Went to the WIPO benchmark sub-page for Nigeria for scores: it publishes all seven pillar scores for Nigeria against Sub-Saharan Africa, lower middle-income and top-10 averages, again with no overall score. Checked the WIPO GII 2024 Nigeria PDF brief (edocs/gii-ranking/2024/ng.pdf): rank 113rd of 133 and pillar ranks only; the GII score appears solely as a plotted axis on the bubble chart, with no readable numeric value in the text. Checked the GII 2024 and 2025 full report pages, the GII 2024 economy-profiles page and the GII 2024 landing page: all describe the framework and leaders but the Nigeria economy-profile table itself was not in the retrieved text, so no overall score could be quoted. countryeconomy.com lists an overall index of 17.10 (2024) and 18.40 (2023), but it is a T5 aggregator and tier rules bar using it for a statistic; recorded in construct_note as context only. Dead end: no admissible page in this set carries Nigeria's single overall GII score, so the statement route was taken.

6.4.name: Agtech venture ecosystem

answer.value: Nigeria has an operating agritech venture ecosystem of digital solution providers for smallholder farmers, supported by incubators, accelerators, angel investors and donors, but only a handful of start-ups have scaled.
answer.source_title: GSMA Mobile for Development, "AgriTech in Nigeria: Investment opportunities and challenges"
answer.quote: Nigeria has seen a rapid growth of agritech companies offering digital solutions aiming to address the challenges faced by smallholder farmers and to improve their livelihoods. While some agritech start-ups have transitioned into established companies, only a handful have scaled.
answer.data_quality_flag: Qualitative landscape summary from a 2020 grey-literature report; the summary page carries no deal counts, funding totals or company counts
answer.construct_note: The GSMA source is explicitly about AGRITECH in Nigeria — farmer-facing digital solutions for smallholders and the investors funding them — which matches the indicator name 'agtech venture ecosystem'. The only QUANTIFIED evidence in the retrieved pages is AgFunder/AgFunderNews 'agrifoodtech' deal flow for Nigeria (reported as 35 deals worth $154 million in 2022, and $45 million in H1 2023), which sits on the wrong side of the unratified definition: 'agrifoodtech' bundles downstream eGrocery, in-store retail tech and restaurant tech with upstream farmer-facing ventures, so it is a measurably broader denominator than 'agtech'. Those figures are additionally published on agfunder.com / agfundernews.com, a T5 vendor/news tier at which statistics are not admissible under the tiering rules, so they are recorded here as context only and are not used as the cell value or as scale evidence.
answer.quality_evidence: Independent T4 sector analysis (GSMA Mobile for Development, 2020) assessing how the Nigerian agritech venture ecosystem actually performs, not how it is intended to perform: it finds that of the agritech companies that have emerged, 'only a handful have scaled', and identifies specific structural failures — 'a challenging business environment, an ecosystem unable to support long-term growth, low levels of agricultural knowledge and skills, and limited access to and awareness of funding opportunities' — plus 'three major funding gaps: limited availability of local capital, a lack of institutional investors investing in agritech and an inability to attract big-ticket investments'. This is third-party performance evidence about the ecosystem's functioning (largely negative), not a self-description by any implementer.
answer.rung_argument: Absent is ruled out: the GSMA page documents that Nigerian agritech companies exist in number. Announced is exceeded: this is not an intention or a launch statement but a retrospective landscape of an existing sector. Adopted is exceeded: the source records not merely that ventures were founded but that 'some agritech start-ups have transitioned into established companies' and that a live funder base — 'incubators, accelerators, angel investors and donors' — is actively deploying capital into them, i.e. the ecosystem is transacting. That places the rung at Operating (base 3). One level is added for quality_evidence: an independent T4 analytical report evaluating how well the ecosystem functions (scaling rate, structural barriers, funding gaps). Total 4.
answer.negative_finding: Level 5 was not proposed because scale_evidence was left empty. No reach figures for the AGTECH venture ecosystem in Nigeria — number of agritech ventures, farmers reached, agritech-specific deal counts or funding volumes — appear in any admissible-tier page retrieved. The only reach-type numbers available (Nigeria's 35 agrifoodtech deals worth $154m in 2022; 38 deals in 2021; $45m in H1 2023) fail on two independent grounds: they are published at T5, where statistics are inadmissible, and they measure the broader 'agrifoodtech' category rather than agtech. Filling scale_evidence with them would import a downstream-inclusive denominator and a non-admissible publisher into this row's score.
answer.search_trail: Reviewed all nine supplied pages in order of likely construct fit. (1) GSMA 'AgriTech in Nigeria: Investment opportunities and challenges' — the only Nigeria-specific, agritech-specific, non-T5 source in the set; used for the cell value and for quality_evidence. (2) AgFunder Africa AgriFoodTech Investment Report landing pages 2022/2023/2024 — Africa-wide totals only ($482m 2021, $636m 2022, $275m 2023, $145m H1 2024); no Nigeria disaggregation on the page text, and Kenya-specific claims there are not evidence about Nigeria. (3) AgFunder Developing Markets report 2025 PDF text — country breakdown lists India, Singapore, Mexico, Vietnam, Chile, Brazil, Indonesia, Kenya; Nigeria does not appear in the retrieved extract, so no 2024 Nigeria figure could be quoted. (4) AgFunderNews data snapshots (Sept 2022, Sept 2023) — these do carry Nigeria figures (38 deals in 2021; 35 deals/$154m in 2022; $45m H1 2023) but are T5 and are 'agrifoodtech', so recorded in construct_note as context only. (5) Disrupt Africa African Tech Startups Funding Report 2025 PDF and funding-report page — the contents list a Nigeria country chapter and an Agri-tech sector chapter, but the retrieved text stops before those chapters, so no Nigerian agri-tech deal or funding number could be copied verbatim; not used. Dead ends: no national statistical office, Nigerian government/NITDA/Ministry of Agriculture, or World Bank/openknowledge source on Nigerian agtech venture activity was among the supplied pages, so no T1-T3 figure was available for this cell.

answer.search_trail: Worked through the nine supplied pages in tier order. Source 1 (NBS census launch, T1) — agricultural statistics, no AI solution; dead end. Source 2 (NBS GHS-Panel Wave 5 data dictionary, T1) — a 'Digital Farming Information' module capturing mobile/SMS/app advisory receipt, but nothing identifying AI-enabled solutions and no published tabulation on this page; dead end for this construct. Source 9 (60 Decibels, T5) — digital farmer services survey of 1,374 Nigerian farmers, but reports digital services generally, not AI-enabled solutions, and is T5. answer.abstain_reason: None of the supplied pages publishes a population-representative percentage of adults with a mobile money account for Nigeria. The only Nigeria-specific mobile money figure in the pages is an unweighted sample frequency in the Findex 2025 microdata catalogue (471 of 1000 cases, 47.1%), which the publisher explicitly states cannot be interpreted as a summary statistic of the population. The WDI series available for Nigeria (63.26, 2024) measures a different construct — account at a financial institution OR with a mobile money provider.
answer.construct_note: Two near-misses were considered and rejected. (1) World Bank WDI 'Account ownership at a financial institution or with a mobile-money-service provider (% of population ages 15+)' lists Nigeria 2024 = 63.26 — this is a combined bank-or-mobile-money measure, not the mobile money account share, and using it would massively overstate the named construct. (2) The Findex 2025 Nigeria microdata variable account_mob ('Has a mobile money account') shows 471 of 1000 cases coded Yes (47.1%), but the catalogue page carries the standard warning that these are raw case counts, not weighted population estimates; the survey uses a weight variable (wgt), so the unweighted share is not the published national statistic. Qualitatively, the IMF selected issues paper describes mobile money in Nigeria as 'still relatively scant' and notes 'relatively low mobile money account ownership', which is not reconcilable with a 47% weighted rate for the same country in an adjacent period, reinforcing that the raw microdata frequency must not be recorded as the indicator value.
answer.quality_evidence: Admissible T1 publishers (World Bank Global Findex / WDI) do produce the named construct as a standard series ('Mobile money account, % age 15+', FX.OWN.MOBL.ZS), but the retrieved pages contain the combined account series instead. The one Nigeria-specific mobile money datum retrieved is a microdata catalogue frequency table carrying an explicit non-inference warning from the publisher.
answer.scale_evidence: Not established. No weighted national percentage of Nigerian adults with a mobile money account appears in the supplied pages for any reference year (2011, 2014, 2017, 2021 or 2024).
answer.rung_argument: No level proposed. A threshold indicator requires a defensible value for the named construct. The only candidate values in the supplied evidence either measure a different construct (63.26 combined bank-or-mobile-money account, WDI 2024) or are disclaimed by their own publisher as non-representative (47.1% unweighted microdata cases). Scoring on either would place the row at level 3 or 4 on evidence that does not support it, so the level is withheld pending retrieval of the Findex mobile money account series for Nigeria.
answer.negative_finding: Withheld rather than scored: no supplied page states a weighted, population-representative percentage of Nigerian adults aged 15+ holding a mobile money account, so even the lowest cut point (10%) cannot be tested against a verified figure.
answer.search_trail: Checked, in order: (1) WDI indicator page FX.OWN.TOTL.ZS — has Nigeria 2024 = 63.26 but the series title is 'Account ownership at a financial institution or with a mobile-money-service provider', a combined measure; rejected on construct grounds. (2) Findex 2025 Nigeria microdata variable page for account_mob — correct construct label ('Has a mobile money account') but only raw case counts (529 No / 471 Yes) with an explicit warning that they cannot be read as population summary statistics; rejected. (3) Findex 2025 Nigeria data dictionary — confirms account_mob and a weight variable exist, but publishes no percentages. (4) Findex 2021 Nigeria microdata catalogue pages (catalog/4688) — study metadata only, no indicator values. 7.12.name: Responsible-AI safeguards (consent, rights)

answer.value: Nigeria has a binding cross-sector responsible-AI safeguard framework: the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 and the NDPC's General Application and Implementation Directive (GAID) 2025, which sets out consent rules, data-subject rights and dedicated articles on emerging technologies, is administered by an operating regulator (registration, audit filing, data-subject access/objection-to-automated-decision-making requests); nothing agriculture- or farmer-specific was found.
answer.source_title: Nigeria Data Protection Commission, Nigeria Data Protection Act (NDP Act) 2023 — General Application and Implementation Directive (GAID) 2025, NDPC/NDP ACT-GAID/01/2025
answer.quote: Article 43: Emerging Technologies
answer.data_quality_flag: Instrument text (arrangement of articles) quoted from the regulator's own published directive; no independent assessment of implementation was available in the retrieved pages.
answer.construct_note: The indicator name — 'Responsible-AI safeguards (consent, rights)' — carries no agriculture qualifier, so a cross-sector regime is judged to satisfy it. The evidence sits on the cross-sector side of the census's open question: the NDP Act 2023 / GAID 2025 consent and data-subject-rights provisions and the National AI Strategy's Pillar 4 ('Ensuring Responsible and Ethical AI Development and Deployment') apply economy-wide. No agriculture- or farmer-specific consent/rights safeguard (e.g. a farmer-data code of conduct, agricultural AI code, or MARD/FMAFS instrument) appears in any retrieved page. If the row is later ratified as requiring agriculture-specific safeguards, this cell should fall to Absent/Announced and the evidence below becomes context only.
answer.rung_argument: Absent is excluded: a written safeguard regime exists (NDP Act 2023; GAID 2025 with Articles 15-27 on principles, lawful bases and consent, Articles 36-40 on exercise of rectification, portability, erasure and complaint rights, and Articles 41-44 on data ethics and emerging technologies). Announced is exceeded: these are not statements of intent but a statute and a regulator-issued directive with an operative authority clause; the National AI Strategy (Sept 2025, FMCIDE/NITDA, T3) additionally names 'Ensuring Responsible and Ethical AI Development and Deployment' as a strategic pillar. Adopted is met and passed: the directive is issued under the Commission's statutory powers and dated March 2025. Operating is proposed because the regulator runs live machinery under it — a published Data Subject Access Request form (forms.ndpc.gov.ng) that lets individuals exercise the 'Right to Withdraw Consent' and 'Right to Object to Automated Decision Making' with a stated 30-day response commitment, plus controller/processor registration, audit filing and published investigations. Operating gives base level 3; both evidence add-on fields are empty, so the level stays at 3.
answer.negative_finding: Level 4 was not proposed because no independent or official evaluation, audit or performance report on how well the consent/rights safeguards actually function for AI systems was found in the retrieved pages — the NDPC pages are the implementer's own description of its intentions and processes, which the scoring rules class as design, not quality. Level 5 was not proposed because no reach figures were found either: no published counts of AI-related data-subject complaints handled, DPIAs filed by AI deployers, enforcement actions under Articles 43-44, or coverage of the regime among deployers. The UNESCO AI Ethics Observatory country profile carries related figures but the domain is tiered T5 here and its cited scores (e.g. ITU GCI 82.40/100) measure cybersecurity, not AI consent/rights safeguards, so they were not used.
answer.search_trail: 1) Checked the two peer-reviewed/T2 items first: the CCSI blog on smallholder AI adoption in Rwanda and Nigeria discusses the need for 'clear rules around data use and standards, as well as safeguards against harm' but states no Nigerian safeguard instrument or figure, and the MDPI 'Responsible AI in Farming' paper is a generic design framework with no Nigeria content — neither is evidence for this cell. 2) National AI Strategy (Sept 2025, T3, ncair.nitda.gov.ng) confirms Pillar 4 on responsible and ethical AI but the retrieved text is executive-summary level with no consent/rights obligations quotable. 3) 2024 draft strategy adds nothing beyond the 2025 final. 4) NDPC pages: the Act download page is navigation chrome only (no Act text); the NDPC internal privacy policy restates consent and S.34/S.35 rights but binds only NDPC itself; the DSAR form evidences an operating rights channel including objection to automated decision-making; the NYIGF news item shows the regulator addressing automated decision-making without human oversight. 5) Settled on the GAID 2025 directive as the binding, quotable instrument. Dead end: no agriculture-specific or farmer-data consent instrument appeared anywhere in the retrieved set, and no evaluation or reach statistics for the regime were present, so both add-on fields were left empty.

7.12.perplexity_lead:
For **Nigeria**, the best published match I found is **not agriculture-specific**; it is a **cross-sector data-protection / responsible-AI safeguard** grounded in the **Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023**, which gives data subjects rights around **consent** and protection from **solely automated decisions**, including the rights to **human intervention**, **express a point of view**, and **contest the decision**[1][4][6].

That means the construct, **as written**, matches the published evidence only if the indicator accepts a **cross-sector regime**. If the indicator requires something **agriculture- or farmer-specific**, then the best available evidence is on the **wrong side** of that question, because the published Nigerian sources I found describe general AI/data-protection safeguards rather than an agriculture-only measure[1][3][4][6].

- The clearest published statement is from **Nigeria’s Data Protection Act 2023**, as summarized by the UNESCO Nigeria profile and AI-law analyses: individuals have rights connected to **consent** and to **not being subject to decisions based solely on automated processing** unless exceptions apply, with safeguards such as **human intervention**

answer.quote: In 2024, 52.2% of women and 74.3% of men in Nigeria had an account
answer.data_quality_flag: Sample survey estimate (Global Findex 2025, Gallup World Poll; Nigeria microdata n=1000 cases), so subject to sampling error; nationally representative, not rural-specific.
answer.construct_note: The quoted figure is sex-disaggregated (female) account ownership for Nigeria, which is exactly what the indicator names. Two caveats bearing on the unratified definition: (a) the underlying WDI series is FX.OWN.TOTL.FE.ZS, 'Account ownership at a financial institution OR with a mobile-money-service provider, female (% of population ages 15+)', which reports 52.22 for Nigeria 2024 — i.e. mobile-money accounts are counted inside the total, the same construct scored separately at 8.4, so mobile money is double-weighted in the FIN column as the census note flags; (b) the corresponding all-adult figure is not the answer to this cell — for context the male figure is 74.3% and the Gender Data Portal notes a 22.1 point male-female gap, larger than the Sub-Saharan Africa gap of 12.1.
answer.quality_evidence: Global Findex 2025 (World Bank Development Research Group with Gallup, Inc.), nationally representative face-to-face survey of adults conducted over calendar year 2024; Nigeria study record NGA_2024_FINDEX_v02_M, DOI 10.48529/d4fc-pm96, geographic coverage 'National Coverage'. The same 52.2/52.22 value appears both on the Gender Data Portal country page and in the WDI series FX.OWN.TOTL.FE.ZS for Nigeria (Most Recent Year 2024, Most Recent Value 52.22).
answer.scale_evidence: Population base is all Nigerian women aged 15 and above; the estimate is national, not disaggregated to rural areas or to agricultural households.
answer.rung_argument: The figure is a single published number for the named construct, so the level follows the cut points arithmetically; the argument here is about the value and its match. Level 1 would require female account ownership below 20% — not the case (52.2). Level 2 would cap it at 40% — exceeded. Level 3 requires the value to exceed the 40 cut, which 52.2 does, and the figure is a T1 official Global Findex/WDI estimate for Nigeria, female-disaggregated, for reference year 2024, so the construct match is direct rather than inferred from an all-adult figure.
answer.negative_finding: Level 4 would require the female figure to exceed 60%. It does not: the published 2024 value is 52.2% (WDI 52.22), nearly eight points short, and the male figure of 74.3% shows the shortfall is specifically female — the 60 threshold is passed by Nigerian men but not by Nigerian women. No admissible source in the retrieved pages publishes a higher female figure for Nigeria.

Dead end: no rural-female or agricultural-household breakdown was found in any retrieved page; none is required by this indicator's name.

The Findex 2025 Nigeria pages supplied are microdata catalogue/variable listings only: they show a household-level phone question (con8) with unweighted case counts explicitly flagged as not interpretable as population statistics, and list a 'female' variable, but publish no cross-tabulated male/female individual phone-ownership rate for Nigeria.
answer.construct_note: Context, not an answer to this cell: the GSMA Mobile Gender Gap Report 2025 landing page states the LMIC-aggregate gender gap in overall mobile ownership was 8% in 2024 and the smartphone gap 14% — these are (i) low- and middle-income-country aggregates across 15 surveyed markets, not Nigeria, and (ii) relative gaps expressed as a percentage of male ownership, which is exactly the basis mismatch the indicator census flags: the indicator name fixes the unit as percentage points, so the GSMA number cannot be transcribed into this cell even if a Nigeria-level version were available in these pages. The one Nigeria-specific gender figure surfaced is in a T5 news headline (technext24: 'Only 39% of Nigerian women own a smartphone'), which is (i) smartphones rather than phones, (ii) a single-sex level with no corresponding male figure from which to compute a gap, and (iii) news tier, which may not carry a statistic. The Findex Nigeria microdata variable con8 asks 'Does anyone in your household currently own a mobile phone?' — household-level ownership, not individual ownership, and therefore not decomposable by respondent sex into a personal-ownership gap.
answer.quality_evidence: Admissible tiers are present in the retrieved set (T1 World Bank Findex microdata catalogue, T4 GSMA), but neither carries the named quantity for Nigeria. answer.value: A randomized controlled trial of the RiceAdvice digital personalized-extension app in Nigeria found that farm households receiving personalized advice increased their yield by 7% and their profit by 10%.
answer.source_title: American Journal of Agricultural Economics (Wiley) — Arouna, Michler, Yergo & Saito, 'One Size Fits All? Experimental Evidence on the Digital Delivery of Personalized Extension Advice in Nigeria'
answer.quote: We find that households who were just given the personalized advice increase their yield by 7% and increase their profit by 10%.
answer.data_quality_flag: Experimental estimate from a single-country RCT with a defined study area; not a national-level impact figure
answer.construct_note: The evidence sits on the correct side of the census's open question: the measured outcomes are yield (+7%) and profit (+10%) from a digital advisory tool (RiceAdvice mobile app) in Nigeria, i.e. yield/income outcomes rather than diffusion or adoption of digital tools. A second Nigerian digital-extension RCT (Oyinbo et al., 'Digital extension, price risk, and farm performance', AJAE 2022) reports that site-specific digital recommendations 'improve fertilizer management practices and maize yields' with 'only incremental increases in investments and net revenues', but the page supplied for it is an IDEAS/RePEc bibliographic listing (T5), so it is recorded here only as corroborating context, not as the quoted source. Other supplied Nigerian impact studies (innovation platforms on maize income, PMC10208796; improved soybean varieties on yield and revenue, PMC9539571) measure non-digital interventions and therefore do not evidence digital-agriculture impact. World Bank APPEALS ISR figures (62.62% productivity increase, 61,171 beneficiaries) are for a general agro-processing project, not a digital service.
answer.quality_evidence: Peer-reviewed randomized controlled trial published in the American Journal of Agricultural Economics, conducted by researchers independent of the implementing body's own reporting, evaluating the effectiveness of a digital decision-support tool and quantifying yield and profit effects: 'We present results from a randomized control trial designed to evaluate the effectiveness of a mobile application that provides personalized advice on rice nutrient management.'
answer.rung_argument: Absent is ruled out: at least one published, country-specific study documents yield and income impacts of a digital agricultural service in Nigeria. Announced is exceeded: the evidence is not a planned or commissioned study but a completed, published one (the IFPRI/FCDO Crop2Cash Nigeria impact evaluation, running Aug 2025–Sep 2026, would be merely 'announced'). Adopted/Operating: documented impact evidence exists in the public domain and is being generated on an ongoing basis for Nigerian digital advisory services (Arouna et al. 2021; Oyinbo et al. 2022), so the rung is Operating (base 3). +1 for quality_evidence, which is filled by an independent peer-reviewed RCT that measures how well the digital tool actually performs on yield and profit, not what it intends to do. Total 4.
